9.7a — Computer Systems: What Runs Your Game

60 frames per second means the machine has 16.67 milliseconds to run YOUR Update, the physics, and a million pixels. Today: the four organs of every computer — and why knowing them turns your tuning instincts into engineering.

Concept Lab ~15 min

The four organs — and what your game asks of each:

OrganJobYour game's demand
CPUExecutes instructions — your C#Every Update: input, Distance checks, cooldowns, FindWithTag
GPUDraws pixels — massively parallelTilemap, sprites, particles, your camera view, 60×
RAMWorking memory — fast, forgets at power-offLoaded scene, all your fields, the tilemap in memory
Storage (SSD/HDD)Persistent — slow, remembersThe .unity files, assets, your whole project (9.4a)

The frame budget. 60 fps = 16.67 ms per frame. Inside that: all Update()s, physics step, culling, and the GPU draw — usually 5–12 ms of CPU work in a game like yours, leaving slack for spikes (a burst of turrets firing). Your deltaTime habits (1.5a) exist because the frame rate is a NEGOTIATION with hardware, not a constant.

The frame pipeline, in order:

1. Input    → your GetAxis/GetKeyDown (Input System)
2. Update  → YOUR code runs (movement, cooldowns, AI ifs)
3. Physics → collision resolution, rigidbody integration
4. Render  → sprites sorted (7.2a layers!) and drawn

That order explains a bug you have MET: the turret's projectile spawns in one frame and damages on a LATER frame's physics pass. Nothing is instant; everything is scheduled.

Socratic

Unity calls Update before physics and FixedUpdate on the physics clock. Why would physics need a FIXED timestep while your Update does not — and which of your systems (cooldown timer vs. AddForce jump) would break if you moved it into the wrong one?

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — watch the budget. Unity's Window → Analysis → Profiler (attach while playing): see the frame time ms by ms. Find your Update cost, the physics cost, the render cost. On a simple scene it is mostly render. Where does the spike happen when all three turrets fire simultaneously?

Step 2 — feel CPU vs GPU. Make each expensive in turn:

  1. CPU: spawn 200 enemies (each has Update + Distance to player). Watch fps fall — the CPU is saturated by per-frame LOGIC
  2. GPU: spawn 200 large sprites over a huge particle burst. The frame drops differently — draw calls, not logic. Read the Profiler's Hierarchy to see which organ is complaining

Step 3 — RAM meets your scene data. Load the overworld: RAM holds it. Load the Platformer scene (5.3a): the old scene UNLOADS — that is the hitch you sometimes see mid-door. The singleton survives because DontDestroyOnLoad says "this one is not scene-RAM anymore."

Bug Hunt: Slow on a friend's laptop

  1. Your game runs 60 fps in the lab but 25 fps on a school Chromebook. Name the organ that likely hurts first for a 2D Unity game — and which knob (quality settings? resolution? particle count?) respects it
  2. FindObjectsByType runs in the lever branch each E press (5.2a). Why is that cheap ON AN E-PRESS and expensive inside Update — and what did you learn about WHERE code runs, not just WHAT it does?
  3. Why does your game take 10 seconds to BUILD but loads instantly in the editor after — and what is warm in RAM that was cold at launch?
  4. The exam classic: "Which is volatile — RAM or storage?" Answer, then explain why your coins reset when you quit (2.1a) using exactly those two words.
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Spec like an engineer

  1. Find your machine's four numbers (About This Mac / dxdiag): CPU speed, RAM GB, GPU name, storage type. Write them next to your game's measured fps — a spec sheet for YOUR build.
  2. Write a minimum-spec sentence for your game: "Playable at ___ fps on a machine with at least ___." How would you FIND the second blank honestly (borrow machines, not vibes)?
  3. Hard: 30 fps vs 60 fps — your deltaTime movement works on both (1.5a proof). But your cooldowns use Time.time — what CHANGES at low fps for a cooldown, if anything — and why is that "correct" (wall-clock vs frame-clock)?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name the four organs with your game's demand on each
  • Read the Profiler and identify CPU vs GPU saturation
  • Explain the frame pipeline order and a bug it predicts
  • Explain volatile RAM vs persistent storage with your own coins
